title: Explain service discovery in depth — service registry, instances, clients, client-side vs server-side discovery, health checks, load balancing/failover, Kubernetes DNS, service mesh, security (registry poisoning, mTLS/Zero Trust), performance (DNS TTL, proxy hops, registry scaling), and multi-region setups.

s1_definition.profdef: Service discovery is the mechanism by which a microservice finds the network location (host and port) of another service at runtime, without those addresses being hardcoded. A service registry holds a live catalog of healthy instances, discovery clients query that catalog to resolve a logical service name into a real endpoint, and health checks keep the catalog accurate as instances start, stop, crash, and scale. It can be done client-side (the caller queries the registry and load-balances itself) or server-side (a load balancer or platform resolves the name on the caller's behalf).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh walks into the National Bank of India and wants to speak to "the loans department." He does not memorize which desk, which floor, or which employee — those change every day as staff come and go. Instead there is a central reception register at the entrance that always knows which loan officers are present and healthy right now. Rajesh asks reception "who handles loans?", reception checks its live register, and points him to an available officer. If an officer goes home sick, reception removes them from the register so nobody is sent to an empty desk. That reception register is the service registry, and the act of asking and being routed is service discovery.
s1_definition.oneliner: Service discovery turns a stable logical name like payment-service into a live, healthy, reachable address, and the registry is the always-updated phone book that makes it possible.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Service discovery is the mechanism by which a microservice finds the network location (host and port) of another service at runtime, without those addresses being hardcoded. A service registry holds a live catalog of healthy instances, discovery clients query that catalog to resolve a logical service name into a real endpoint, and health checks keep the catalog accurate as instances start, stop, crash, and scale. It can be done client-side (the caller queries the registry and load-balances itself) or server-side (a load balancer or platform resolves the name on the caller's behalf).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh walks into the National Bank of India and wants to speak to "the loans department." He does not memorize which desk, which floor, or which employee — those change every day as staff come and go. Instead there is a central reception register at the entrance that always knows which loan officers are present and healthy right now. Rajesh asks reception "who handles loans?", reception checks its live register, and points him to an available officer. If an officer goes home sick, reception removes them from the register so nobody is sent to an empty desk. That reception register is the service registry, and the act of asking and being routed is service discovery.

**One line to remember:** Service discovery turns a stable logical name like payment-service into a live, healthy, reachable address, and the registry is the always-updated phone book that makes it possible.

sections.s2_technical:
A service registry is a database of currently running instances keyed by service name. Each instance, when it starts, registers itself with its host, port, and metadata, and then sends periodic heartbeats to prove it is alive. Netflix Eureka, HashiCorp Consul, and etcd are common registries. In Spring Cloud with Eureka, an instance registers using `@EnableEurekaClient` behavior and the client sends a renew heartbeat every thirty seconds by default; if the registry misses several heartbeats it evicts the instance. For example, a payment service exposing an endpoint registers as `payment-service` with address `10.0.3.14:8080`.

A discovery client is the code inside the caller that resolves a name to an instance. In client-side discovery the caller fetches the full list of healthy instances and picks one itself using a load-balancing rule. Spring Cloud LoadBalancer does exactly this: a call to `lb://payment-service` fetches instances and chooses one. For example, `webClientBuilder.build().get().uri("lb://payment-service/api/v1/settle")` lets the framework resolve and balance. In server-side discovery the caller just hits a stable virtual address, such as a load balancer or Kubernetes Service, and that layer consults the registry and forwards the request, so the caller carries no discovery logic.

Health checks are what keep the registry honest. A liveness check answers "is the process alive?" and a readiness check answers "can it accept traffic right now?" A service that is alive but still warming its cache should report not-ready so no requests are routed to it yet. Load balancing and failover ride on top of discovery: because the registry only lists healthy instances, the load balancer naturally spreads requests across them, and if one dies the registry prunes it so traffic shifts to the survivors automatically.

In Kubernetes the registry is effectively built in. A Kubernetes Service gives a stable DNS name like `payment-service.prod.svc.cluster.local`, and kube-proxy or the CNI routes to the healthy Pod endpoints behind it. This is server-side discovery via DNS; the application just calls the DNS name and never touches a registry API. A service mesh like Istio or Linkerd goes further by injecting a sidecar proxy next to each Pod that handles discovery, load balancing, retries, and mutual TLS transparently, so application code stays unaware.

Security matters because the registry is a trust anchor. If an attacker can register a fake instance (registry poisoning), they can hijack traffic meant for the real service, so registration must be authenticated and the registry access-controlled. Zero Trust and mutual TLS (mTLS) ensure that both caller and callee prove their identity with certificates, which a mesh automates. On performance, DNS-based discovery is subject to TTL caching, so a short TTL means faster failover but more lookups; proxy hops in a mesh add a small latency per call but buy you consistent policy; and the registry itself must scale and stay consistent under thousands of instances, which is why registries like Eureka deliberately favor availability and may serve slightly stale data rather than refuse. Multi-region setups typically run a registry per region with federation, prefer same-region instances to keep latency low, and fail over cross-region only when a whole region's instances are unavailable.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the account service must call the payment service to settle a transfer. In the early days a junior developer hardcoded the payment service address as `http://10.0.3.14:8080` inside the account service.

Problem 1 — the payment service was redeployed on a new node and got a new IP, so every transfer started failing with connection refused even though the payment service was perfectly healthy. This is exactly the problem service discovery solves: instead of a fixed address, the account service asks a registry for the current healthy address of `payment-service` and always gets a live endpoint.

Problem 2 — during a sale, the bank scaled the payment service from one instance to four to handle load, but the account service kept hammering the single old IP, so three new instances sat idle while one was overwhelmed. This is exactly how discovery with load balancing works: the registry lists all four healthy instances, and the discovery client spreads requests across them, so adding capacity instantly helps.

Problem 3 — one payment instance crashed mid-day. Without discovery, one in four transfers failed. With discovery, the registry noticed the missed heartbeats, evicted the dead instance, and the caller stopped routing to it automatically.

The mini-project simulates this. We build an in-memory `ServiceRegistry` that stores healthy instances per service name and prunes stale ones using heartbeats. We build a `DiscoveryClient` that resolves a name to one instance using round-robin load balancing. We build a `PaymentServiceInstance` that registers and heartbeats. We build an `AccountService` that uses discovery to settle a transfer for Rajesh. The demo registers four payment instances, settles several transfers to show balancing, crashes one instance, and shows discovery routing around the failure.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four payment instances at 10.0.3.11 through 10.0.3.14, and a request to transfer fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1: Each payment instance starts and calls `registry.register`, so the registry now lists four healthy entries under the name payment-service, each with a fresh heartbeat timestamp.

Step 2: The account service receives a transfer request. It does not know any payment address, so it calls `discovery.resolve("payment-service")`.

Step 3: The discovery client asks the registry for healthy instances. The registry filters out anything stale and returns all four. The client applies round-robin, returning 10.0.3.11 for the first call, 10.0.3.12 for the second, and so on. The data at this point is just a chosen address string.

Step 4: The account service performs the settlement against the chosen instance and logs success. The balances conceptually change at the payment service, but the key output is which instance handled each call, proving the load is spread.

Step 5: Instance 10.0.3.13 crashes and stops heartbeating. Time passes beyond the expiry window. `registry.evictStale` runs, sees the stale timestamp, and removes 10.0.3.13, logging an eviction.

Step 6: New transfers call resolve again. Now only three healthy instances remain, so the client balances across 10.0.3.11, 10.0.3.12, and 10.0.3.14 only. No request is ever sent to the dead instance.

    │
    ├─ BEFORE crash (4 healthy)         ├─ AFTER evict (3 healthy)

sections.s6_takeaway:
Service discovery is the runtime mechanism that lets one microservice find another without hardcoding network addresses. At its heart is a service registry, which is a live catalog of every running instance keyed by a logical service name. When an instance starts it registers itself with its host and port, and it sends periodic heartbeats so the registry knows it is still alive; if the heartbeats stop, the registry evicts that instance. Discovery is the act of resolving a logical name like payment-service into a real, healthy, reachable address at the moment a call is made.

In my banking projects the account service needs to call the payment service to settle transfers. We never hardcode the payment address because instances are redeployed, scaled, and occasionally crash. Instead the account service uses a discovery client that asks the registry for the currently healthy payment instances and then load-balances across them, usually round-robin. When we scaled payment from one instance to four during a sale, discovery immediately spread traffic across all four with no config change, and when one instance crashed, the registry pruned it after missed heartbeats so no further requests were routed to the dead node.

There are two flavors I always distinguish. In client-side discovery the caller itself fetches the instance list and picks one, which is what Spring Cloud LoadBalancer does when you call lb://payment-service. In server-side discovery the caller just hits a stable address like a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service and that layer consults the registry on its behalf. In Kubernetes this is effectively built in through Service DNS names, and a service mesh like Istio pushes discovery, load balancing, retries, and mutual TLS into a sidecar so the application code stays unaware.

The nuances I mention to show depth are security, performance, and multi-region. Security-wise, the registry is a trust anchor, so registration must be authenticated to prevent registry poisoning, and Zero Trust with mutual TLS ensures both sides prove identity. Performance-wise, DNS TTLs trade failover speed against lookup volume, mesh proxy hops add small latency for consistent policy, and the registry itself must scale, which is why Eureka favors availability and may serve slightly stale data combined with client retries. For multi-region we run a registry per region, prefer same-region instances for latency, and fail over across regions only when a whole region is unavailable.

The one line I leave the interviewer with is that the registry is the always-updated source of truth about instances, and discovery is the glue that turns a logical service name into a live, healthy endpoint, which is what makes a microservices system elastic and self-healing.
